chapters.title: Chapter 4: Estimating How Much Capital a Strategy Can Actually Absorb

lessons.title: Worked Example: Estimating Capacity for a Nifty 50 Mean-Reversion Strategy

children.text: Chapter 1 argued that a Nifty 50 index fund can absorb enormous inflows without a real capacity problem. This lesson tests whether that holds for an active strategy trading the same 50 stocks, and shows exactly where it stops holding.
The Strategy: Short-Term Mean Reversion on Nifty 50

The strategy buys Nifty 50 stocks that have underperformed their sector by more than a set threshold over the past 5 trading days, expecting the gap to partly close, and holds each position for around 10 trading days before exiting. The universe is rescreened weekly, and the book typically holds around 15 positions at a time.

stats.label: Average holding period
stats.context: Implies portfolio turnover T of roughly 25x per year (250 trading days / 10)

stats.label: Average concurrent positions
stats.context: The typical size of the reversion basket at any time

stats.label: Universe
stats.context: The most liquid stocks traded on the NSE

children.text: Real ADV varies stock by stock even within the Nifty 50, but for a first-pass estimate, use illustrative typical figures for a Nifty 50 constituent: ADV of Rs 200 crore, daily volatility of 1.5%, and a calibration constant Y of 0.7. Keep the same 2% annual impact cost budget used in the previous lesson.
Step 2: Per-Stock Capacity, Adjusted for Turnover

Using the capacity formula from the previous lesson, AUM_max equals ADV times (C divided by T times Y times sigma), squared: 200 crore times (0.02 divided by 25 times 0.7 times 0.015), squared, which comes out to roughly Rs 1.16 crore of capacity per stock. Despite trading the most liquid names on the NSE, the strategy's own turnover of 25 times a year crushes the per-stock number down to just over a crore.

With around 15 positions held at once, and treating each position as independently capacity-constrained, a simplification that ignores any shared crowding from Chapter 3, total portfolio capacity is roughly 15 times Rs 1.16 crore, about Rs 17.4 crore.
Why "Nifty 50" Does Not Automatically Mean Unlimited Capacity

body.text: Chapter 1 said a Nifty 50 index fund can absorb huge inflows because it is not searching for a scarce mispricing and turns over its book only when the index itself changes, effectively turnover near zero. This mean-reversion strategy trades the exact same 50 stocks and still ends up with a real, calculable ceiling around Rs 17 to 18 crore, because its turnover of roughly 25 times a year interacts multiplicatively with liquidity, exactly the relationship from the previous lesson. Liquidity of the underlying stocks was never the only variable. Turnover matters just as much, and here it matters more.

children.text: The sensitivity to holding period is dramatic. Extend the average hold from 10 trading days to 60, turnover falls from roughly 25x to roughly 4x a year, and per-stock capacity rises from Rs 1.16 crore to about Rs 45.35 crore, pushing total portfolio capacity to roughly Rs 680 crore, about 39 times higher, using identical stocks and an identical cost budget.

body.title: Total Portfolio Capacity: Fast vs Slow Reversion
Recompute Per-Stock Capacity at a Different Holding Period
body.prompt: Using the same inputs (ADV Rs 200 Cr, sigma 1.5%, Y 0.7, cost budget 2%), if the average holding period is stretched to 20 trading days instead of 10, implying a portfolio turnover of roughly 12x per year, what is the per-stock capacity, in Rs Cr? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: AUM_max = 200 x (0.02 / (12 x 0.7 x 0.015))^2 = 200 x (0.02 / 0.126)^2 = 200 x 0.1587^2 = 200 x 0.02520 = Rs 5.04 Cr per stock, about 4.3 times the 10-day figure even though holding period only doubled.

body.text: Trading the most liquid stocks in India does not, by itself, buy you high capacity. A fast strategy on Nifty 50 stocks can have a lower ceiling than a patient strategy on names half as liquid. Holding period, not just the universe you trade, decides how much capital a strategy can actually hold.

points: A full capacity estimate combines per-stock ADV, portfolio turnover, and the number of concurrent positions, not liquidity alone.
A high-turnover strategy on the most liquid stocks in the market, the Nifty 50, can still end up with a modest capacity ceiling once turnover is factored in.

Because capacity scales with the square of turnover, extending holding period is often the single most powerful lever for raising a strategy's capacity, more powerful than switching to a more liquid universe.

Aggregating per-stock capacity across concurrent positions gives a useful first-pass portfolio capacity estimate, though it assumes positions behave independently, an assumption Chapter 3's crowding risk can violate.
